newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank drops support for Euro campaign - paper.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank drops support for Euro campaign - paper.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer changed his mind and turned down a request by the German government to support a campaign for the future single European currency, a German newspaper said on Saturday.

The Berliner Zeitung said Tietmeyer had first agreed to back the government in an advertising campaign aimed at drumming up popular support for the Euro, the proposed single European currency that could be introduced in 1999.

But Tietmeyer had recently written a letter explaining that, as the head of the powerful central bank, he could not take part in such an advertising campaign because he needed to maintain his independence.
Neither the chancellery nor the Bundesbank could confirm the report.
A spokesman for the Bundesbank, however, said the central bank stands behind the government's efforts to create a currency union based on stability-oriented policies.

"The Bundesbank has been involved in its own information offensive for the Euro for several months," the Bundesbank spokesmans said. "We have been publishing information brochures aimed at the general public that go deeply into the subject."
He added that Tietmeyer has also written numerous articles and given many speeches about the Euro.
The newspaper report said that Tietmeyer's refusal to take part in the government's information campaign had raised doubts in Bonn about the Bundesbank's commitment to the Euro.
The rejection could also cause international investors to question the central bank's stance on the Euro, the newspaper quoted government officials in Bonn as saying.

The series of advertisements are to be a key part of the government's efforts to enlighten Germans about the Euro. Prominent economic experts and leaders in Germany are being asked to offer their observations on the single currency.
Opinion polls have consistently shown that even though politicians and industrialists favour the the Euro, most ordinary Germans are sceptical about it and want to keep their cherished D-marks.

The Bundesbank, which sits in Frankfurt and is largely free of government interference, enjoys widespread respect and credibility in Germany. The support from Tietmeyer was considered vital for the advertising campaign.
Tietmeyer was harshly criticised this week by former Chancellor Helmut Schmidt for his strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for European currency union.
In an open-letter in the newspaper Die Zeit, Schmidt blasted Tietmeyer's stance on EMU as counter-productive to the success of monetary union.
"I regard you (Tietmeyer) as the most important opponent of currency union. This is not meant as an insult, but your stance shows a lack of strategic vision," Schmidt wrote.
Schmidt continued that Tietmeyer's "insistent and penetrating" speeches made Germans generally unpopular in Europe, as they give the impression that Germans are "power-hungry and too-powerful."

Separately, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said in a speech on Saturday not enough was being done to stress the advantages of European monetary union and that public debate focused too much on fears the Euro may be weak.
"It is time to go on the offensive in discussing the advantages of European Union and not to spread fear of a weak currency," Welteke said.
